Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Sources conflict sharply: Cable.co.uk-based reporting (2022, via Global Citizen) put Namibia's 1GB cost at US$10.52, among the world's most expensive, and Context/TRF (2022) also describes Namibia's mobile data as 'among world's highest'; the undated bestbroadbanddeals.co.uk table cites only $1.20. The original comment ('<1% GNIpc') is also internally inconsistent with its own Value Code 4 (1-2% band), which corresponds instead to Code 5. Given contradictory, undated evidence, recalculated to 0 (Unknown) pending verification against ITU ICT Price Baskets or current A4AI data. Flagged for human review.

Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited figure of 15.92 kbit/s per internet user (2023) falls within the 'Low (5-19 kbit/s)' band, not 'Moderate (20-49)' as originally coded — an internal inconsistency in the original entry (comment and code did not match the stated scale). Historical ITU-based data (theglobaleconomy.com, 2012-2016 avg 10.76 kbit/s) is consistent with a low-bandwidth position. Recalculated to Code 2.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: PeeringDB is itself the authoritative primary registry for this indicator; no fresher or contrary evidence found for the Namibia IXP's participant count. Retained Code 4, but independent verification of participant/traffic numbers (e.g. via Af-IX) is recommended.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: DataReportal/GSMA Intelligence confirms 2.67m cellular connections = 87.1% of population (early 2025), consistent with Code 5 (70%+). However, this is a connections figure, not the unique-subscriber metric the variable specifies (DataReportal itself cautions connections can exceed unique subscribers); GSMA's unique-subscriber percentage could not be independently sourced in this pass. Retained Code 5 as plausible for Namibia's small, competitive market, but flagged for human review to confirm against GSMA Intelligence's unique-subscriber series specifically.

Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: On direct inspection, the DataReportal figure cited (92.9%) refers to the share of mobile connections that are 'broadband' (3G/4G/5G-capable), not the share of connections using smartphone devices — a different metric from the one this variable requires, and DataReportal explicitly warns against treating it as a device/adoption proxy. No genuine smartphone-adoption percentage for Namibia (e.g. from GSMA Intelligence) was found in this pass. Recalculated to 0 (Unknown) pending sourcing of the correct metric; flagged for human review.

Definition: The availability and presence of major cloud service providers (hyperscale and regional) operating in or serving the country with local or near-local infrastructure. Cloud availability determines access to scalable computing resources for government, business, and startups.
Value Name: Served remotely from distant regions only (>100ms latency)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: AWS (af-south-1, Cape Town) and Microsoft Azure (South Africa North/West, Johannesburg & Cape Town) both operate hyperscale regions in South Africa, the same sub-region as Namibia. An academic latency study measuring from nearby African countries to these South African regions recorded roughly 45-84ms, i.e. under the >100ms threshold used to define Code 2. This better matches Code 3 ('Regional cloud availability zone nearby, same sub-region') than the originally stated Code 2. Recalculated to 3.

This meets Code 3 ('at least one Tier III facility'), not Code 2. Recalculated to 3.

Definition: Percentage of total electricity generation from renewable sources (hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, biomass). Indicates energy sustainability and potential for distributed power solutions relevant to ICT infrastructure in off-grid areas.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: World Bank WDI (EG.ELC.RNEW.ZS) records Namibia's renewable electricity output at 93.37% of total generation (2021), and Ember-sourced data (via countryeconomy.com) shows a renewable generation share of 96-98% across 2018-2024, driven mainly by the Ruacana hydro plant and growing solar. Both independent sources place the figure far above the originally cited ~40% and outside the 10-24% band entirely. Recalculated to Code 5 (75%+) based on domestic generation mix as strictly defined by the variable; note this reflects Namibia's own generation only and not its heavy reliance on imported (more fossil-heavy) electricity to meet total demand — flagged for human review given the scale of the change and this nuance.

This is also inconsistent with the original comment's own '~37pp' figure, which would actually fall in the 21-40pp band (Code 3). Given the boundary sensitivity, retained Code 2 as the closer fit to 40.9pp but flagged for human review rather than asserted with confidence.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
Comments: 32% mobile internet gap SSA, similar Namibia. [GSMA](https://www.gsma.com/solutions-and-impact/connectivity-for-good/mobile-for-development/blog/the-mobile-gender-gap-report-2024/)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original source cited a Sub-Saharan Africa-wide GSMA average (32%) and merely asserted it was 'similar' for Namibia, without country-specific evidence — precisely the single-source/non-specific problem flagged for corroboration. The best Namibia-specific data found (Afrobarometer Round 8, 2020, as cited in an Internet Society Namibia report) shows Namibia is the only African country with a gender gap in favour of women: 46% of women vs 39% of men use the internet regularly (-7pp gap), i.e. near parity. This would recalculate to Code 5 (<10% gap), a large change from the original Code 2. Given the data is from 2020 and the finding is a striking outlier, this is flagged for human review rather than treated as a settled confirmation.
